sources_note: Georgia statutes read on law.justia.com (2025 Code of Georgia) through a Chrome tab (Justia challenges curl); DDS pages, SC Code chapters (scstatehouse.gov copies saved by run-2586), GOHS pages and the GOHS 2024 Speeding Traffic Safety Facts PDF, NHTSA, AAA Foundation, FMCSA and the eCFR versioner API read directly. Negligence-per-se, citation-admissibility, comparative-fault and punitive-damages findings are reused from facts-1740, facts-2586 and facts-1756 (verified 2026-09-23/24).

verifiedClaims.claim: a Super Speeder designation triggers an extra $200 state fee that many drivers do not learn about until after their court date — and failure to pay results in automatic license suspension
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(b)-(c) (2025 Code of Georgia, via Justia); Georgia DDS, Reinstatement FAQs - Super Speeder, Q1 and Q8
verifiedClaims.note: Statute verbatim: 'the department shall administer and collect a fee of $200.00 from any driver who is convicted'; non-payment 'shall result in the suspension of the driver's license or driving privileges'. DDS Q8 confirms the court does not collect it: 'the Department of Driver Services (DDS) is responsible for the administration and collection of the $200 Super Speeder fee.'

verifiedClaims.claim: The legal doctrine of negligence per se means that violating a speeding law can establish automatic fault in a personal injury claim.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The legal doctrine of negligence per se means that proof a driver broke the speed limit establishes that the driver breached a duty of care — the injured person still has to prove the speed caused the crash and the injuries
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Central Anesthesia Associates, P.C. v. Worthy, 254 Ga. 728, 333 S.E.2d 829 (Ga. 1985); Whitlaw v. Kroger Co., 306 S.C. 51, 410 S.E.2d 251 (S.C. 1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1740 / facts-2586. 'Automatic fault' overstates: Georgia Supreme Court — 'negligence per se supplies only the duty and breach of duty elements of a tort, and the plaintiffs must still prove a causal connection (proximate cause) ... as well as their damages'; Whitlaw — violation 'is not conclusive of liability'. The Cornell Wex link resolves and law.cornell.edu is on the outbound allowlist; keep the link, change the sentence.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia's Super Speeder Law (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(b)) was enacted in 2010 to target the most dangerous speeding behavior on state roads.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia's Super Speeder Law (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(b)) was enacted in 2009 and took effect January 1, 2010
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189 History: 'enacted by Ga. L. 2009, p. 679, § 11/HB 160'; GOHS Super Speeder Law page: 'Since January 1st, 2010 the Super Speeder Law has been in effect in Georgia'
verifiedClaims.note: The statute was passed in the 2009 session (HB 160) and became effective 2010-01-01. The History line lists no later amendment; the 2010 and 2025 Justia texts of subsections (b)-(e) are identical. Subsection pinpoint (b) is correct for the definition and fee.

verifiedClaims.claim: 75 mph or faster on a two-lane road or highway, or 85 mph or faster on any road or highway in Georgia, regardless of the number of lanes
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(b): '85 miles per hour or more on any road or highway or 75 miles per hour or more on any two-lane road or highway, as defined in Code Section 40-6-187'; DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q1
verifiedClaims.note: Verbatim match. Same thresholds in the excerpt, key takeaways, the comparison table and faq:0.

verifiedClaims.claim: The designation applies automatically upon conviction — it is not a separate charge filed by the officer. The Super Speeder surcharge is assessed by the Georgia Department of Driver Services (DDS) after the conviction is reported
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(b) ('Such a driver, upon conviction, shall be classified as a super speeder'), (c) (DDS notifies 'within 30 days after receipt of a qualifying ticket and notice of conviction'); DDS FAQ Q2, Q8
verifiedClaims.note: DDS Q2: 'If the DDS receives notification of your conviction ... you will be notified by first class mail of the $200 Super Speeder fee.' Optional: add that the statute gives DDS 30 days from receiving the conviction to send the notice.

verifiedClaims.claim: The law was specifically designed to fund Georgia's trauma care network.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(e): fees 'deposited in the general fund of this state with the intent that these moneys be used to fund a trauma care system in Georgia'; cross-reference to the Georgia Trauma Care Network Commission, T. 31, C. 11, A. 5
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate; the money goes to the general fund with a stated legislative intent, not a dedicated trust — 'intended to fund' is the honest verb if the refresher touches the sentence.

verifiedClaims.claim: Approximately 66% of trauma patients treated at Georgia hospitals are victims of motor vehicle collisions
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Approximately 60% of trauma-care patients in Georgia are crash-related, according to the Governor's Office of Highway Safety
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Georgia Governor's Office of Highway Safety, Super Speeder Law page: 'approximately sixty-percent of all trauma-care-patients are crash-related'
verifiedClaims.note: No primary source for 66% was located (trauma.georgia.gov carries no such figure). GOHS's own Super Speeder page says roughly 60%; attribute it to GOHS. The GOHS page dates from the law's launch, so if the refresher prefers, drop the percentage and keep only the funding purpose, which the statute supports.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia averages roughly one speed-related traffic fatality per day, underscoring the public safety rationale behind the enhanced penalties.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Speeding was a factor in 339 of Georgia's 1,403 traffic deaths in 2024 — 24% of the total, or nearly one a day — according to the Governor's Office of Highway Safety
verifiedClaims.sourceName: GOHS, 2024 Speeding Georgia Traffic Safety Facts (published Aug 2026, FARS 2024): 'Twenty-four percent (24%) of all traffic fatalities (339 out of 1,403) were speeding-related in 2024'; '1,312 fatal crashes ... Nearly one out of every four fatal crashes (24%) involved at least one driver who was speeding'
verifiedClaims.note: The one-a-day claim is the GOHS Super Speeder page's 2010 slogan; the 2024 figure (339 / 366 days) still supports it. Replace the slogan with the dated figure and the GOHS attribution. National context if wanted: NHTSA — 11,288 speeding-related deaths in 2024, 29% of all traffic fatalities (https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/speeding).

verifiedClaims.claim: Some drivers pay the fine online without appearing in court, which constitutes a guilty plea.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Some drivers pay the fine online without appearing in court; under O.C.G.A. § 40-13-58 that is treated as an admission of guilt, the court reports it as a conviction, and it counts for Super Speeder purposes
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-13-58 and annotations (Agic v. MARTA, 334 Ga. App. 679 (2015): paying the citation without appearing = acknowledging guilt under § 40-13-58); DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q1-Q2 (fee follows any reported conviction)
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1740. The mechanism is bond forfeiture 'construed as an admission of guilt', not a formal plea; the practical point (it is reported as a conviction and triggers the fee) is right. Minor reword plus the statute.

verifiedClaims.claim: DDS reviews the conviction and, if the speed qualifies, sends a notice of the $200 Super Speeder fee to the driver's address on file.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(c): 'Notice shall be provided by the department to the offender by first-class mail to the address shown on the records of the department'; DDS FAQ Q2
verifiedClaims.note: Verified.

verifiedClaims.claim: 120-day payment window: The driver has 120 days from the date of the notice to pay the $200 fee.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: DDS gives the driver 120 days from the date of its notice to pay the $200 fee (the statute itself, O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(c), sets the deadline at 90 days after the notice is received)
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(c): 'Failure to pay the fee imposed by this Code section within 90 days after receipt of the notice shall result in the suspension'; Georgia DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q2-Q3: 'You will have 120 days from the date of the notice to pay the fee to DDS'
verifiedClaims.note: Most consequential Georgia finding. The statute (identical text in the 2010 and 2025 codes) says 90 days after receipt; DDS, which administers the fee under § 40-6-189(d), tells drivers 120 days from the notice date on its FAQ and (per the FAQ) on the mailed notice. The post's 120 days matches what a driver will actually be told, so keep it as the operative number but stop presenting it as the statute's number: name DDS as the source and add the 90-day statutory text in one clause. Same treatment wherever '120 days' appears (steps 5-6, the suspension section, the out-of-state section, faq:1). The excerpt and key takeaways can stay at 120 days as DDS practice.

verifiedClaims.claim: License suspension if unpaid: Failure to pay within 120 days results in automatic license suspension.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Failure to pay within DDS's 120-day window results in suspension of the driver's license or Georgia driving privilege
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(c); DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q3: 'Failure to pay the Super Speeder fee to DDS within 120 days of the notice date will result in the suspension of your license, permit, or driving privilege in Georgia.'
verifiedClaims.note: See the 120-day entry above; wording change only.

verifiedClaims.claim: Base speeding fine$150–$500+Set by local court; varies by jurisdiction and speed
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Base speeding fine: capped by statute for a first offense — no more than $125 for 15-18 mph over, $150 for 19-23 over, $500 for 24-33 over (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-1(b)); 34 or more over falls under the general misdemeanor maximum of $1,000 (O.C.G.A. § 17-10-3); local courts set the amount within those caps and add their own surcharges
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-1(b)(4)-(6) (2025 Code of Georgia, via Justia); O.C.G.A. § 17-10-3(a)(1)
verifiedClaims.note: '$150–$500+' traces to no statute. § 40-6-1(b) verbatim: first-offense speeding fine 'By more than 14 but less than 19 miles per hour shall not exceed $125.00; By 19 or more but less than 24 ... $150.00; By 24 or more but less than 34 ... $500.00' (and $0 / $25 / $100 for 5-or-less / 6-10 / 11-14 over). A Super Speeder at 85 in a 70 zone is only 15 over, so the statutory cap there is $125 — the table's $150 floor is wrong for the commonest case. Replace the range with the caps or with 'varies; capped by O.C.G.A. § 40-6-1(b) for most speeds'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Court costs and fees$50–$200Administrative fees assessed by the court
verifiedClaims.note: No primary source for a $50–$200 range; Georgia's statutory add-ons (e.g., the § 15-21-73 and § 15-21-131 surcharges) are percentage- and court-specific and were not verified this run. Keep the row only as 'varies by court' with no dollar figures, or remove it.

verifiedClaims.claim: Super Speeder surcharge$200Assessed by DDS after conviction
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(b); DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q1
verifiedClaims.note: Verified. DDS Q6: a separate $200 fee is owed for each qualifying conviction.

verifiedClaims.claim: License reinstatement fee$50Only if license is suspended for non-payment
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(c) ('a fee of $50.00 shall be assessed, payable upon the application for reinstatement'); DDS Reinstatement Fees table: 'Super Speeder $50.00 **after payment of the $200.00 Super Speeder Fee'
verifiedClaims.note: Verified in statute and on the DDS fee table. Same figure in the suspension section and faq:1.

verifiedClaims.claim: Insurance increase$500–$2,000+/yearRate increases typically last 3-5 years
verifiedClaims.note: No primary source (insurer, regulator or statute) for the dollar range or the 3-5 year duration. Keep a qualitative row ('Insurance increase — likely; amount and duration depend on the insurer') or remove it.

verifiedClaims.claim: Points on license2-6 pointsDepends on speed over limit; 15 points = suspension
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Points on license: 2 points for 15-18 mph over, 3 for 19-23, 4 for 24-33, 6 for 34 or more (no points for 14 or less over); 15 points in any 24-month period suspends the license
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-5-57(c)(1)(A)(v)-(viii) and (c)(1)(B) (2025 Code of Georgia, via Justia); DDS Points and Points Reduction page ('A driver with 15 points in a 24 month period will have their license suspended')
verifiedClaims.note: The 2-6 range and the 15-point trigger are right; add the schedule so the comparison table's '6 points for 25+ over' can be corrected (see below). DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q5: no additional points are added for the Super Speeder designation itself or for the non-payment suspension. § 40-5-57 annotations (In the Interest of R.G., 272 Ga. App. 276 (2005)): under § 40-5-51(a) no points are assessed against a non-resident.

verifiedClaims.claim: A single Super Speeder conviction can cost a driver $3,000 to $10,000 or more over the following years when insurance premium increases are included.
verifiedClaims.note: Built on the unsourced insurance row; no primary source. Remove the sentence or reduce it to 'the insurance cost usually dwarfs the fee' without figures.

verifiedClaims.claim: speeding 15 mph or more over the limit in a commercial vehicle is a serious traffic violation under federal regulations, and two serious violations within three years triggers a 60-day CDL disqualification
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 49 CFR § 383.51(c), Table 2: 'Speeding excessively, involving any speed of 24.1 kmph (15 mph) or more above the regulated or posted speed limit' — second conviction 'in a separate incident within a 3-year period while operating a CMV' = 60 days; third = 120 days (eCFR, current as of 2026-09-01)
verifiedClaims.note: Verbatim match via the eCFR versioner API. Optional precision: the 60-day disqualification applies to a second serious violation committed while driving a CMV; a second one in a personal vehicle disqualifies only if it also suspends the driver's license. Cite as '49 CFR § 383.51'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Driving on a suspended license in Georgia is a misdemeanor criminal offense (O.C.G.A. § 40-5-121) that carries penalties of up to $1,000 in fines and up to 12 months in jail for a first offense.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-5-121(a) (2025 Code of Georgia, via Justia): first conviction is a misdemeanor punished 'by imprisonment for not less than two days nor more than 12 months, and there may be imposed in addition thereto a fine of not less than $500.00 nor more than $1,000.00'
verifiedClaims.note: Maxima are correct. Optional: add the minimums (two days' jail, $500 fine if a fine is imposed) and the additional six-month DDS suspension under § 40-5-121(b)(1). Same statute in faq:1.

verifiedClaims.claim: Repeat offenses carry mandatory minimum jail sentences.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-5-121(a): second and third convictions within five years — high and aggravated misdemeanor, 'imprisonment for not less than ten days nor more than 12 months', fine $1,000-$2,500; fourth or subsequent — felony, one to five years
verifiedClaims.note: Verified. Even a first offense carries a two-day minimum (1992 Op. Att'y Gen. No. U92-10 notes it may be suspended or probated).

verifiedClaims.claim: If you are involved in a car accident while driving on a suspended license, the suspension can be used as evidence of negligence and may affect your ability to recover compensation for your own injuries.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Driving on a suspended license does not by itself prove you drove negligently in the crash — Georgia's courts treat a licensing violation with no causal connection to the collision as irrelevant and inadmissible — but it can complicate your case and your insurance coverage, so tell your lawyer about it early
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Central Anesthesia Associates, P.C. v. Worthy, 254 Ga. 728 (Ga. 1985), discussing Fielding v. Driggers, 126 Ga. App. 365 (licensing-statute violation with no causal connection 'irrelevant and inadmissible')
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1740's licensing-statute finding. As written the sentence tells an injured reader that a suspended license is evidence of negligence; in Georgia the unlicensed/suspended status is inadmissible on negligence unless it caused the crash. Reword as shown or cut the sentence.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia DDS accepts Super Speeder payments online through the DDS website, by mail with a check or money order, or in person at a DDS Customer Service Center.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q7: online via DDS Online Services; by mail with 'check, money order or cashier's check made payable to DDS' to Dept. of Driver Services, CSLR, P.O. Box 80447, Conyers, GA 30013; in person at a Customer Service Center (cash and credit/debit cards only — 'We do not accept checks, money orders, or cashiers checks' in person)
verifiedClaims.note: Verified. Optional: note that in-person payment is cash or card only.

verifiedClaims.claim: Payments must be received — not just postmarked — within the 120-day window.
verifiedClaims.note: Neither § 40-6-189 nor the DDS FAQ addresses postmark versus receipt. Remove the sentence; 'pay well before the deadline' is the safe advice without a rule the source does not state.

verifiedClaims.claim: Drivers who have moved and not updated their address with DDS may never receive the notice, but the suspension still takes effect.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(c): mailed notice to 'the address shown on the records of the department' is 'adequate notification' and 'No other notice shall be required to make the driver's license suspension effective.'
verifiedClaims.note: Directly supported by the statute; worth citing.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia's Super Speeder Law applies equally to out-of-state drivers convicted of qualifying speeding offenses on Georgia roads. If you are a South Carolina resident, tourist, or commercial driver passing through Georgia, the same $200 surcharge and 120-day payment requirement apply.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q4: 'Out of state drivers are subject to the same requirements as Georgia drivers.'
verifiedClaims.note: Verified. The '120-day' phrase follows the treatment above (DDS's window).

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia suspends your privilege to drive in Georgia (even though it cannot suspend your home state license)
verifiedClaims.sourceName: DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q4: 'If you do not pay the Super Speeder fee, the DDS will impose a suspension of your non-resident driving privilege in Georgia.'; O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(c) ('driver's license or driving privileges')
verifiedClaims.note: Verified.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia notifies your home state through the Driver License Compact, and most states — including South Carolina — take reciprocal action
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia reports the suspension to your home state's licensing agency, which decides whether to take action of its own; South Carolina belongs to the Driver License Compact (S.C. Code § 56-1-610 et seq.), but the compact only requires it to give effect to Georgia convictions for vehicular homicide, DUI, felonies involving a vehicle and hit-and-run — anything else, including an unpaid fee, is at SCDMV's discretion
verifiedClaims.sourceName: DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q4: 'The DDS will then report the suspension to your home state's licensing authority which would then decide to take additional action, if any.'; S.C. Code § 56-1-650(A), (C) (Driver License Compact, Article IV as enacted in South Carolina)
verifiedClaims.note: 'Most states ... take reciprocal action' is not sourced and overstates: DDS itself says the home state decides. § 56-1-650(A) lists the four conviction types a member state must give effect to; (C) leaves other reported convictions to § 56-1-320. A Super Speeder non-payment suspension is not even a conviction. Reword as shown; keep 'may' in faq:3, which is already hedged correctly.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina may suspend your SC license based on Georgia's notification, creating a dual-state problem
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina decides for itself whether to act on Georgia's report; do not assume it will ignore it
verifiedClaims.sourceName: DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q4; S.C. Code § 56-1-650(C)
verifiedClaims.note: 'May' is acceptable; the bullet only needs to stop implying a routine reciprocal suspension once the preceding bullet is fixed.

verifiedClaims.claim: Driving through Georgia with a suspended Georgia driving privilege is a criminal offense
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-5-121(a): any person who drives on a public highway 'at a time when his or her privilege to so drive is suspended, disqualified, or revoked shall be guilty of a misdemeanor'
verifiedClaims.note: Verified; the statute reaches suspended driving privileges, not only Georgia-issued licenses. Annotations require proof the driver had actual or legal notice of the suspension.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina does not have an equivalent "Super Speeder" law, but the state imposes its own significant penalties for excessive speeding
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-1520(G) (speeding penalties tiered by mph over: $15-$25 for up to 10 over; $25-$50 for more than 10 but less than 15; $50-$75 for 15 to less than 25; $75-$200 or up to 30 days for more than 25 over) — no state surcharge provision exists in Title 56, Chapter 5, Article 15
verifiedClaims.note: Correct. The tiered fine schedule in § 56-5-1520(G) is the South Carolina statute the post should be citing for 'excessive speeding' penalties; it is currently absent from the post.

verifiedClaims.claim: Reckless driving (S.C. Code § 56-5-2920): Driving at a speed or in a manner that endangers persons or property is classified as reckless driving.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Reckless driving (S.C. Code § 56-5-2920): driving 'in such a manner as to indicate either a wilful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property' is reckless driving
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-2920 (South Carolina Legislature)
verifiedClaims.note: Section number correct; the statutory standard is wilful or wanton disregard, not 'endangers'. Wording fix.

verifiedClaims.claim: While South Carolina does not set a specific speed threshold, courts routinely treat speeds of 25+ mph over the limit as reckless driving.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina sets no speed threshold for reckless driving; 25 mph or more over the limit is instead the top tier of the speeding statute — $75 to $200 or up to 30 days in jail for a first offense (S.C. Code § 56-5-1520(G)(4)) and six points (§ 56-1-720) — and whether a given speed was also 'wilful or wanton' is a charging decision for the officer and the court
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-2920 (no threshold); § 56-5-1520(G)(4); § 56-1-720 ('25 m.p.h. or above the posted limits — 6')
verifiedClaims.note: No South Carolina opinion or statute makes 25-over reckless per se, and the SC pack bars unsourced 'courts routinely' attributions. The 'no threshold' half is right. Same fix in faq:2 and in the comparison-table cell 'No specific speed; typically 25+ over'.

verifiedClaims.claim: A first offense carries a fine of $25-$200 or up to 30 days in jail.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-2920: 'a fine of not less than twenty-five dollars nor more than two hundred dollars or by imprisonment for not more than thirty days'; second offense within five years adds a three-month license suspension
verifiedClaims.note: Verbatim match.

verifiedClaims.claim: Racing on highways (S.C. Code § 56-5-2190): Engaging in speed competitions on public roads carries enhanced penalties including fines up to $200, up to 30 days in jail, and potential vehicle impoundment.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Racing on public roads (S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1590 and 56-5-1620): a driver convicted of racing or a contest for speed faces a $200 to $600 fine or two to six months in jail, or both, plus a one-year driver's license revocation; an owner who knowingly lets the car be used for racing faces up to $100 or 30 days and a three-month suspension of license and registration
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-1590 ('Unlawful to race or assist in racing on public roads'); § 56-5-1620 ('Penalties for racing; revocation or suspension of drivers' licenses and registrations')
verifiedClaims.note: Most consequential South Carolina finding. § 56-5-2190 does not exist (Article 13 runs 56-5-2110 to 56-5-2180, all turning and signalling rules). The racing statute is § 56-5-1590 with penalties in § 56-5-1620, and every figure in the bullet is wrong: the fine is $200-$600 (not 'up to $200'), jail is two to six months (not 'up to 30 days'), the license is revoked for a year, and there is no impoundment provision. Same phantom citation is not in the meta surfaces, so the fix is body-only.

verifiedClaims.claim: Points system: South Carolina assesses points for speeding convictions — 2 points for 10 mph over, 4 points for 10-25 mph over, and 6 points for 25+ mph over. Accumulating 12 or more points triggers license suspension.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina assesses 2 points for speeding up to 10 mph over, 4 points for more than 10 but less than 25 over, and 6 points for 25 or more over (S.C. Code § 56-1-720); 12 points brings a three-month suspension, rising to six months at 20 or more (§ 56-1-740), with points counting at full value for a year and half value for the second year (§ 56-1-750)
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-1-720 (schedule); § 56-1-740(A) (twelve points 'indicates disrespect and disregard'; 12-15 points three months, 16-17 four, 18-19 five, 20+ six); § 56-1-750 (computation)
verifiedClaims.note: Point values and the 12-point trigger are right; '2 points for 10 mph over' should read 'up to 10 mph over' and the 4-point band is 'more than 10 but less than 25'. Also fixes the comparison-table cell '12 points in 24 months', which is a gloss on § 56-1-750's half-value rule rather than a statutory window.

verifiedClaims.claim: Insurance consequences: South Carolina insurers use a surcharge system where speeding convictions result in percentage-based premium increases that last for three years from the conviction date.
verifiedClaims.note: No statute in Title 38, Chapter 73 (read on scstatehouse.gov) prescribes a percentage surcharge or a three-year duration for speeding convictions; the uniform merit-rating plan the sentence recalls was repealed with the 1999 auto-insurance reform. Remove or reduce to 'expect a premium increase'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Reckless driving speed thresholdNo specific speed; officer discretionNo specific speed; typically 25+ over
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina cell: 'No specific speed; 25+ over is the top speeding tier (§ 56-5-1520(G))'
verifiedClaims.note: Drop 'typically 25+ over' for the reason given above. The Georgia cell asserts nothing statutory and can stand.

verifiedClaims.claim: Points for 25+ mph over limit6 points6 points
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: 4 points for 24-33 mph over, 6 points only at 34 or more (O.C.G.A. § 40-5-57(c)); South Carolina: 6 points (S.C. Code § 56-1-720)
verifiedClaims.note: The Georgia cell is wrong: 25 over is in the 24-33 band (4 points); 6 points starts at 34 over. South Carolina's 6 is correct.

verifiedClaims.claim: License suspension trigger15 points in 24 months12 points in 24 months
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: 15 points in any consecutive 24-month period (O.C.G.A. § 40-5-57(c)(1)(B)); South Carolina: 12 points, counted at full value for 12 months and half value for months 12-24 (S.C. Code §§ 56-1-740, 56-1-750)
verifiedClaims.note: Georgia cell verified verbatim. South Carolina has no '24 months' window in the suspension statute; the two-year figure comes from the half-value/expiry rule in § 56-1-750. Minor wording fix.

verifiedClaims.claim: Statute of limitations (injury claim)2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33)3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530)
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1740 / facts-1756 (verified 2026-09-24); matches the writer-profile jurisdiction table.

verifiedClaims.claim: Comparative fault ruleLess than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33)Less than 51% at fault
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g); Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (S.C. 1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1740 / facts-2586; matches the profile table. Optional '(Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.)' in the South Carolina cell — never § 15-38-15.

verifiedClaims.claim: In both states, violating a traffic law such as a speed limit constitutes negligence per se — meaning the violation itself establishes the duty and breach elements of a negligence claim.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Central Anesthesia Associates v. Worthy, 254 Ga. 728 (Ga. 1985) ('negligence per se supplies only the duty and breach of duty elements'); Whitlaw v. Kroger Co., 306 S.C. 51 (S.C. 1991); O.C.G.A. § 51-1-6
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1740 / facts-2586. This sentence states the doctrine correctly (duty and breach only); it is the intro sentence and faq:4 that overreach.

verifiedClaims.claim: A Super Speeder conviction or any speeding ticket creates strong evidence that the at-fault driver was negligent, simplifying the burden of proof for the injured victim.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The speeding ticket and the conviction themselves generally cannot be shown to the jury in either state; what carries the claim is proof of the speed — the crash reconstruction, event-data-recorder and witness evidence, and, if the driver pleaded guilty or in Georgia simply paid the ticket without appearing, that admission
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Howard v. Lay, 259 Ga. App. 391 (2003) (convictions inadmissible in a civil action; guilty plea admissible as an admission); Eubanks v. Waldron, 263 Ga. App. 75 (2003); O.C.G.A. § 40-13-58; S.C. Code § 56-5-6160 ('No evidence of conviction of any person for any violation of this chapter shall be admissible in any court in any civil action'); Samuel v. Mouzon, 282 S.C. 616 (S.C. Ct. App. 1984)
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1740 / facts-2586 (the same admissibility error found on three sibling posts). A 'Super Speeder conviction' is exactly the evidence both states exclude; the guilty plea is what comes in. Same correction in faq:4 and in the closing section's 'use the driver's speeding violation — including a Super Speeder conviction — as powerful evidence', which should become 'use the evidence of the driver's speed — and any guilty plea to the ticket — as powerful evidence'.

verifiedClaims.claim: a vehicle traveling at 85 mph carries roughly three times the kinetic energy of one traveling at 50 mph
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Arithmetic: kinetic energy scales with the square of speed; (85/50)^2 = 2.89
verifiedClaims.note: Follows from the physics stated in the same sentence; no external source needed. GOHS's Super Speeder page states the same idea ('Crash forces double on impact with every 10mph increase in speed above fifty').

verifiedClaims.claim: In Georgia, you cannot recover if you are 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). In South Carolina, the threshold is 51%.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g); Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co. (S.C. 1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1740 / facts-2586; matches the profile table.

verifiedClaims.claim: If the speeding driver's conduct rises to the level of willful misconduct, wantonness, or conscious indifference to consequences, punitive damages may be awarded.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(b) (clear and convincing evidence of 'willful misconduct, malice, fraud, wantonness, oppression, or that entire want of care which would raise the presumption of conscious indifference to consequences'); S.C. Code § 15-32-520(D) ('wilful, wanton, or reckless conduct')
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1756. 'May' is the right hedge; speeding alone rarely meets either standard (Colonial Pipeline Co. v. Brown, 258 Ga. 115 (1988): 'Negligence, even gross negligence, is inadequate').

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1), while South Carolina caps them at three times compensatory damages or $500,000, whichever is greater (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(g)), with no cap where the driver intended to cause harm or drove while substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs (§ 51-12-5.1(f)); South Carolina caps them at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530(A)), a floor indexed each year and set at $739,245 for 2026, and lifts the cap entirely where the driver was substantially impaired (§ 15-32-530(C))
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(f), (g); S.C. Code § 15-32-530(A), (C), (D); S.C. Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Office, Punitive Damage Award Limitation – Inflation Component memo, 2026-02-03
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1756 / facts-2586 (verified 2026-09-24). Both caps and section numbers are correct; add the pinpoints, the indexed 2026 floor and the impairment exceptions, which matter on a speeding post because street racing and DUI are the fact patterns that reach punitive damages. Same fix in faq:5. Profile rule: never say South Carolina has no cap.

verifiedClaims.claim: Commercial trucks require 20-40% more stopping distance than passenger vehicles.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: A loaded tractor-trailer traveling at 55 mph needs about 196 feet to stop in ideal conditions, compared with 133 feet for a passenger vehicle — nearly half again as far, according to FMCSA
verifiedClaims.sourceName: FMCSA, CMV Driving Tips - Following Too Closely: 'The average stopping distance for a loaded tractor-trailer traveling at 55 mph (in ideal conditions) is 196 feet, compared with 133 feet for a passenger vehicle.'
verifiedClaims.note: No primary source for '20-40%'; FMCSA's own figures imply about 47% farther at 55 mph. Replace the percentage range with the FMCSA feet figures.

verifiedClaims.claim: Speed differential between motorcycles and other vehicles is a leading cause of fatal motorcycle crashes in both Georgia and South Carolina.
verifiedClaims.note: No GOHS, SCDPS or NHTSA source ranks 'speed differential' as a leading cause of fatal motorcycle crashes in either state. Replace with a claim-free sentence (speeding leaves riders no margin to react) or drop the bullet's second clause.

verifiedClaims.claim: A pedestrian struck by a vehicle at 40 mph has an 85% chance of death, compared to a 10% chance at 20 mph.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: A pedestrian's risk of death reaches 10% at an impact speed of 23 mph, 50% at 42 mph and 90% at 58 mph, according to the AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety
verifiedClaims.sourceName: AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety, Impact Speed and a Pedestrian's Risk of Severe Injury or Death (Tefft, 2011): 'risk of death for a pedestrian reaches 10% at an impact speed of 23 mph, 25% at 32 mph, 50% at 42 mph, 75% at 50 mph, and 90% at 58 mph'
verifiedClaims.note: The post's 85%-at-40-mph figure does not match the AAA study (the standard U.S. source), which puts 40 mph at roughly 45%; the older UK curve the post seems to echo is not a primary U.S. source. Replace with the AAA figures and attribution.

verifiedClaims.claim: At Roden Law, our car accident lawyers represent injury victims across Georgia and South Carolina on a contingency fee basis — you pay nothing unless we win your case.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: profiles/writer-profile.md trust signals; rodenlaw.com homepage ('100% contingency. You pay nothing unless we win.')
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1740. The tel: href +18447378587 is 1-844-RESULTS and matches the profile.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia's Super Speeder Law adds a $200 surcharge for driving 75+ mph on a two-lane road or 85+ mph anywhere, with license suspension if unpaid within 120 days.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(b); DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q1-Q3 (120 days from the notice date)
verifiedClaims.note: Published as the Article description. Thresholds and fee verified; '120 days' is DDS's stated window and is what the driver is told, so it can stand in a one-line description once the body explains the 90-day statutory text. Optional: 'within DDS's 120-day window'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia's Super Speeder Law (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(b)) imposes an additional $200 surcharge on drivers convicted of 75+ mph on two-lane roads or 85+ mph anywhere, with automatic license suspension for non-payment within 120 days.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(b)-(c); DDS Super Speeder FAQ
verifiedClaims.note: Verified; section symbol renders correctly on this post (no 'SS' defect). Same 120-day note as the excerpt.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina has no equivalent law but treats excessive speeding as reckless driving (S.C. Code § 56-5-2920).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina has no equivalent law; it fines speeding on a tiered scale that tops out at $75-$200 or 30 days in jail for 25+ mph over (S.C. Code § 56-5-1520), and can charge reckless driving (§ 56-5-2920) where the speed shows wilful or wanton disregard for safety
verifiedClaims.note: Renders above the article. 'Treats excessive speeding as reckless driving' states a rule that does not exist; the reckless-driving statute has no speed component.

verifiedClaims.claim: Speeding violations establish negligence per se in injury claims under both states' modified comparative fault rules.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Proof that a driver was speeding establishes negligence per se — the duty and breach elements — in both states; the injured person must still prove causation and damages, and both states then apply modified comparative fault (Georgia bars recovery at 50% fault, South Carolina at 51%)
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Central Anesthesia Associates v. Worthy (Ga. 1985); Whitlaw v. Kroger Co. (S.C. 1991); O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g); Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co. (S.C. 1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Negligence per se and comparative fault are separate doctrines; the sentence fuses them ('under ... comparative fault rules'). Reword.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under Georgia's Super Speeder Law (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(b)), a driver convicted of traveling 75 mph or faster on a two-lane road or 85 mph or faster on any road is classified as a Super Speeder and must pay an additional $200 state surcharge on top of the original speeding fine and court costs.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(b) ('In addition to any other fines or penalties imposed by any local jurisdiction'); DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q1
verifiedClaims.note: Verified verbatim; renders into FAQPage structured data. Nothing to change.

verifiedClaims.claim: If you fail to pay the $200 Super Speeder fee within 120 days of the Georgia DDS notice, your driver's license is automatically suspended. Reinstatement requires paying the original $200 fee plus a $50 reinstatement fee. Driving on a suspended license is a misdemeanor under O.C.G.A. § 40-5-121.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q3 (120 days of the notice date; $50 reinstatement fee in addition to the $200); O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(c); O.C.G.A. § 40-5-121(a)
verifiedClaims.note: Every figure and citation verified. The answer attributes the 120 days to the DDS notice, which is accurate; optional parenthetical '(the statute sets 90 days after receipt, O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(c))'. Renders into FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: No. South Carolina does not have a Super Speeder equivalent. However, excessive speeding may be charged as reckless driving under S.C. Code § 56-5-2920, which carries fines up to $200 or 30 days in jail for a first offense. Speeds of 25+ mph over the limit are routinely treated as reckless driving.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No. South Carolina does not have a Super Speeder equivalent. Speeding is fined on a tiered scale, and 25 mph or more over the limit carries $75 to $200 or up to 30 days in jail for a first offense plus six license points (S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1520, 56-1-720). Excessive speed can also be charged as reckless driving under S.C. Code § 56-5-2920 — $25 to $200 or up to 30 days — but the statute sets no speed threshold.
verifiedClaims.note: Renders into FAQPage structured data. The reckless-driving fine range is right; 'routinely treated as reckless driving' is unsourced and should go.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. Georgia's Super Speeder Law applies equally to out-of-state drivers. If you fail to pay the $200 fee, Georgia suspends your privilege to drive in the state and notifies your home state through the Driver License Compact, which may result in your home state taking additional action against your license.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: DDS Super Speeder FAQ Q4 (same requirements; suspension of non-resident driving privilege; report to home state 'which would then decide to take additional action, if any'); S.C. Code § 56-1-610 et seq. (Driver License Compact)
verifiedClaims.note: Correctly hedged ('may'); matches DDS. Optional: 'notifies your home state's licensing agency' rather than naming the compact as the channel, since DDS does not say which mechanism it uses. Renders into FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: A Super Speeder conviction or any speeding ticket can establish negligence per se in a personal injury claim, meaning the traffic violation automatically proves the duty and breach elements of negligence. This creates strong evidence supporting the injured victim's claim for damages.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Proof that the driver was speeding can establish negligence per se, meaning the violation supplies the duty and breach elements of negligence; the injured person still has to prove the speed caused the crash and the injuries. The ticket and the conviction themselves are generally not admissible in a civil case in Georgia or South Carolina, but a guilty plea to the ticket can be used as an admission.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Central Anesthesia Associates v. Worthy (Ga. 1985); Whitlaw v. Kroger Co. (S.C. 1991); Howard v. Lay, 259 Ga. App. 391 (2003); S.C. Code § 56-5-6160; Samuel v. Mouzon (S.C. Ct. App. 1984)
verifiedClaims.note: Renders into FAQPage structured data, so the admissibility error is published twice. Same correction as the body's 'strong evidence' sentence.

verifiedClaims.claim: Potentially yes. If the speeding driver's conduct rises to willful misconduct or conscious indifference to consequences, punitive damages may be available. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1), while South Carolina caps them at three times compensatory damages or $500,000 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases, with no cap where the driver intended to cause harm or was substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(f)-(g)). South Carolina caps them at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 — a floor indexed to inflation and set at $739,245 for 2026 — and removes the cap where the driver was substantially impaired (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1756 / facts-2586. Standard and caps correct; add 'whichever is greater' (the body has it, the FAQ dropped it), the indexed floor and the impairment exceptions. Renders into FAQPage structured data.

recommendedEdits: Intro: change 'can establish automatic fault' to 'establishes that the driver breached a duty of care — you still have to prove the speed caused the crash'; keep the Cornell link.
What Is a Super Speeder: 'was enacted in 2010' -> 'was enacted in 2009 (HB 160) and took effect January 1, 2010'.

What Is a Super Speeder: replace '66% of trauma patients' with GOHS's 'approximately 60% of trauma-care patients are crash-related' (attributed to GOHS) or drop the percentage; replace 'roughly one speed-related traffic fatality per day' with 'Speeding was a factor in 339 of Georgia's 1,403 traffic deaths in 2024 — 24%, nearly one a day (GOHS, 2024 Speeding Traffic Safety Facts)'.
How It Works, step 2: 'which constitutes a guilty plea' -> 'which O.C.G.A. § 40-13-58 treats as an admission of guilt and the court reports as a conviction'.

How It Works, steps 5-6, the suspension section and the out-of-state section: keep 120 days but attribute it to DDS ('DDS gives you 120 days from the date of its notice') and add once, in step 5, '(the statute itself, O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189(c), sets the deadline at 90 days after you receive the notice — pay early)'.

Penalty table, base fine row: replace '$150–$500+' with the § 40-6-1(b) first-offense caps ($125 for 15-18 over, $150 for 19-23, $500 for 24-33; $1,000 misdemeanor maximum under § 17-10-3 at 34+) and cite the statutes in the Notes cell.

Penalty table: remove the dollar figures from the court-costs row ('varies by court') and from the insurance row ('likely; amount depends on the insurer'), or delete both rows; delete the '$3,000 to $10,000' sentence.

Penalty table, points row: '2-6 points, depends on speed' -> '2 (15-18 over), 3 (19-23), 4 (24-33), 6 (34+); 15 points in 24 months = suspension (O.C.G.A. § 40-5-57)'; add that the Super Speeder fee itself adds no points (DDS FAQ Q5).
CDL sentence: add the citation '49 CFR § 383.51'.

License Suspension section: keep the § 40-5-121 penalties (optionally add the two-day / $500 minimums); rewrite 'the suspension can be used as evidence of negligence' to say a suspended license does not by itself prove negligence in the crash and is generally inadmissible on that question in Georgia unless it caused the collision.
How to Pay: delete 'Payments must be received — not just postmarked — within the 120-day window'; optionally note in-person payment is cash or card only.

Out-of-State section, bullets 2-3: replace 'most states — including South Carolina — take reciprocal action' with 'your home state's licensing agency decides whether to act on Georgia's report; South Carolina is a Driver License Compact member (S.C. Code § 56-1-610 et seq.) but the compact only obliges it to honor Georgia convictions for vehicular homicide, DUI, vehicle felonies and hit-and-run'.

SC section, reckless-driving bullet: quote the statutory standard ('wilful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property'); delete 'courts routinely treat speeds of 25+ mph over the limit as reckless driving' and add the § 56-5-1520(G) tier for 25+ over ($75-$200 or up to 30 days, six points).

SC section, racing bullet: change the citation to 'S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1590, 56-5-1620' and the penalties to '$200 to $600 fine or two to six months in jail, or both, plus a one-year license revocation'; delete 'potential vehicle impoundment'. § 56-5-2190 does not exist.

SC section, points bullet: '2 points for 10 mph over' -> '2 points for up to 10 mph over', '4 points for 10-25' -> '4 points for more than 10 but less than 25'; add that 12 points brings a three-month suspension (S.C. Code § 56-1-740).
SC section: delete the 'Insurance consequences' bullet (percentage surcharge / three years) or reduce it to 'expect a premium increase'.

Comparison table: SC reckless cell -> 'No specific speed; 25+ over is the top speeding tier'; GA points cell for 25+ over -> '4 points (24-33 over); 6 points at 34+'; SC suspension cell -> '12 points (full value for 12 months, half for the next 12)'.

How Speeding Affects Claims, negligence per se: replace 'A Super Speeder conviction or any speeding ticket creates strong evidence' with the admissibility-correct version (ticket and conviction generally inadmissible in both states; proof of speed and any guilty plea are what come in); add '(Howard v. Lay; S.C. Code § 56-5-6160)'.
Punitive damages paragraph and faq:5: add pinpoints (g)/(f), the impairment exceptions in both states, 'whichever is greater' in the FAQ, and South Carolina's indexed floor ($739,245 for 2026).

Accident Types: truck bullet -> FMCSA's 196 ft vs 133 ft at 55 mph; motorcycle bullet -> drop the 'leading cause' claim; pedestrian bullet -> AAA Foundation figures (10% at 23 mph, 50% at 42 mph, 90% at 58 mph) with attribution.

Attorney Help section: 'including a Super Speeder conviction — as powerful evidence' -> 'including any guilty plea to the speeding ticket — as powerful evidence', since the conviction itself is inadmissible.

Key takeaways: rewrite the South Carolina sentence (tiered speeding fines under § 56-5-1520; reckless driving only where wilful or wanton) and the negligence-per-se sentence (duty and breach only; comparative fault is separate).
FAQ 2 and FAQ 4: apply the same South Carolina and admissibility corrections as the body; FAQ 0, 1 and 3 stand as written.

statuteCitations.name: Classification as super speeder; fees — (b) $200 fee at 85+ anywhere / 75+ on a two-lane road, classification upon conviction; (c) DDS notice within 30 days, suspension for non-payment within 90 days after receipt, $50 reinstatement fee, first-class mail to address of record is adequate notice; (e) fees to general fund intended for trauma care. Enacted Ga. L. 2009, p. 679, § 11/HB 160; text unchanged since.

Point system — (c)(1)(A)(v)-(viii) speeding: 15-18 over 2 points, 19-23 over 3, 24-33 over 4, 34+ over 6; (c)(1)(B) suspension at 15 points in any consecutive 24-month period; annotation: no points for non-residents (§ 40-5-51(a))

Driving while license suspended or revoked — first conviction misdemeanor, 2 days to 12 months, fine $500-$1,000; second/third within five years high and aggravated misdemeanor, 10 days minimum, $1,000-$2,500; fourth felony 1-5 years; (b)(1) additional six-month suspension, $210/$200 reinstatement
Violations of chapter a misdemeanor; (b) first-offense speeding fine caps: $0 (5 or less over), $25 (6-10), $100 (11-14), $125 (15-18), $150 (19-23), $500 (24-33)
Punishment for misdemeanors generally — fine not to exceed $1,000 or confinement not to exceed 12 months, or both

Failure to appear after posting a cash bond on a traffic citation 'shall be construed as an admission of guilt' (annotations: Agic v. MARTA — paying without appearing acknowledges guilt; Howard v. Lay — conviction inadmissible, guilty plea admissible)
Recovery for breach of a legal duty (statutory basis of negligence per se)
Apportionment of damages; plaintiff barred at 50 percent or more (g)
Punitive damages — clear-and-convincing standard (b); specific-intent and substantial-impairment exceptions (f); $250,000 cap (g)
Injuries to the person — two-year limitation

Maximum speed limits; (G) first-offense speeding fines tiered by mph over: up to 10 over $15-$25; more than 10 but less than 15 $25-$50; 15 to less than 25 $50-$75; more than 25 over $75-$200 or up to 30 days; (H) citation must state the speed
Reckless driving — 'wilful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property'; $25-$200 or up to 30 days; three-month suspension for a second offense within five years; no speed threshold
Unlawful to race or assist in racing on public roads (the racing statute the post mis-cites as '§ 56-5-2190', which does not exist)

Penalties for racing — driver: $200-$600 or two to six months, or both, and one-year license revocation; owner who acquiesces: up to $100 or 30 days and three-month suspension of license and registration
Evidence of conviction inadmissible in civil action
Point schedule — speeding: no more than 10 over 2; more than 10 but less than 25 over 4; 25 or above 6; reckless driving 6 (as amended by 2025 Act No. 40, eff. 2025-09-01)
Suspension on points — twelve points; 12-15 three months, 16-17 four, 18-19 five, 20+ six; applies to nonresident driving privileges
Computation of points — full value for 12 months, half value 12-24 months, not counted after 24 months
Driver License Compact — short title (South Carolina is a member; §§ 56-1-610 to 56-1-690)

Driver License Compact, Article IV — home state must give effect to reported convictions for vehicular homicide, DUI, vehicle felonies and hit-and-run; other reported convictions governed by § 56-1-320
Three-year limitation, incl. (5) injury to the person
Punitive damages — clear and convincing evidence of wilful, wanton or reckless conduct (D)
Punitive damages cap — greater of 3x compensatory or $500,000 (A); uncapped for intent to harm, felony or substantial impairment (C); annual CPI adjustment, $739,245 in 2026 (D)

CDL disqualification — Table 2 serious traffic violations: speeding 15 mph or more over the limit; second conviction within three years while operating a CMV = 60 days, third = 120 days (verified via the eCFR versioner API, current through 2026-09-01)
